text: Hello, this is Grete. Mama has come home hurt, and something important was left behind by the steps. This is the last week of the novel, and the last week of your essay. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapters 13 and 14, and write your conclusion. Today’s question: what does brave running look like when you don’t know exactly why you’re running?

This week, read like a detective with two boxes. One box holds what could really have happened in Denmark in 1943. The other holds what the author shaped to make a good story. Make your two columns. When you aren’t sure where something goes, write the question down. The Afterword, at the end of the week, will help you check.

The model is a short sentence about running through the woods. The sentence to fix has three words in it that sound almost alike. Decide whether each one is the right twin for its spot. Then find the place where one thought ends and the next one begins, and give each thought a capital.

This week’s word work is about words that sound exactly alike. Say them out loud and you can’t tell them apart. Only the spelling shows which one the writer meant. Nobody gives you the rule first. Hunt for the twins, and work out for yourself how a reader is supposed to know.

Have you ever seen a whole street of windows light up, one candle at a time? This week’s three roots are about shape and about bending, and every right word lights a candle in a window. Some words take the shape root, and some take a bending root. Before you choose, think about what the word is doing.

Four words for the last week of the book. Two of them are about fitting a shape and bending back. Two are about the careful work you’ll do with the Afterword: putting two things side by side, and deciding at the end. Read each sentence, take the word apart, and make a guess before you flip.

Read this sentence out loud and listen. Several words in it have a twin, a word that sounds exactly the same but is spelled differently and means something else. Tap every one. Then try to say the rule. If your ear can’t tell the twins apart, what can?

Same hunt, different sentence. Your ear won’t help you here, so slow down and look. Which words have a sound-alike twin? Tap them. Then think about how you’ll remember which spelling goes with which meaning. Some people make up a little trick for each pair.

Today’s Courage Watch is about being the one who is there. When I was ten, our neighbor fell on the stairs, and her baby was crying alone upstairs. No grown-up was home. I wasn’t brave, only nearest, so I went up. Annemarie isn’t the oldest or the strongest. She is the one who can go. Watch what she decides.

Chapter 13 starts at dawn, with Mama on the ground at the edge of the meadow. Watch what Annemarie finds near the steps, and who decides what to do about it. Then, on the path in Chapter 14, listen to the story Annemarie tells herself as she runs. Why that story, on this path?

Here is one plain sentence: Annemarie ran toward the path. Say it three new ways. Give it a new beginning, swap in a stronger running word, and add a detail about how she ran. The sentence keeps its bones. But each version shows a slightly different girl running into the woods.

Now you write. The questions ask what Mama tells Annemarie to do, and why, and then for one small detail that shows Annemarie is scared and keeps going anyway. The last one asks you to hold this scene up against the real history from Week 15. Then you write your essay’s conclusion.

The third question is the week’s big one. Lowry gives us one girl on one path. The real rescue had hundreds of people, on many paths and many boats. Find one way this scene is like what really happened, and one way it’s different. Both answers can be true at once.

Today you write the ending of your essay. A good conclusion doesn’t just say, the end. It says your claim again in fresh words, names how your character changed, and then looks forward, out of the book and into the real world. Three moves. Sam shows you how first. Then you try.

My mother read us that story from a book with a red cover, and I knew every word. Years later, walking home alone after dark, I said it to myself under my breath, all the way to our door. A story you know by heart is good company when you are frightened. Annemarie seems to think so too.
Conform. To fit in, to match a shape.
Reflect. To bend back, like light, or a thought.
Flexible. Able to bend. Four windows are lit.
